```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE)
```

```{r}
library(fpp2)
housing <- read.csv("HOUSTNSA.csv")
housing_ts <- ts(housing$HOUSTNSA, start = c(1959, 1), frequency = 12)
plot(housing_ts)
```
```{r}
stl_decomp <- stl(housing_ts, s.window = "periodic")
plot(stl_decomp)
```
```{r}
housing_sa <- seasadj(stl_decomp)
plot(housing_ts)
lines(housing_sa, col = "red")
```

The seasonally adjusted series removes the recurring seasonal effects from the original housing starts data. The adjusted series still shows substantial fluctuations, including a sharp decline around 2008–2010 and a gradual recovery afterward. This suggests that changes in housing starts are driven by both seasonal patterns and longer-term movements.
```{r}
f_stl <- forecast(stl_decomp, h=24)
f_stl
plot(f_stl)
```
```{r}
decomp_housing <- decompose(housing_ts)
plot(decomp_housing)
attributes(decomp_housing)
seasadj(decomp_housing)
```

The decomposition results show that U.S. housing starts have clear seasonal patterns and significant long-term fluctuations. Both STL and decomposition reveal a sharp decline around 2008–2010, followed by a gradual recovery. After removing seasonality, the underlying movements become easier to observe. The 24-month STL forecast suggests continued seasonal fluctuations without a strong upward or downward trend, although the wide prediction intervals indicate uncertainty.
